newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Free trade vision shines brighter after WTO parley.
newsitem.headline: Free trade vision shines brighter after WTO parley.

text.p: The vision of global free trade, long scorned as a hopeless dream, this week took shape as a genuine possibility by the middle of the 21st century.
And the body that will manage the transition, the fledgling World Trade Organisation, emerged as a powerful new actor on the world economic stage.
Decisions taken at the WTO's first ministerial conference clearly pointed the way to a future with tariffs all gone and other barriers to commerce torn down.

"In pursuit of the goal of sustainable growth and and development for the common good, we envisage a world where trade flows freely," said a declaration by ministers from the body's 128 member countries.
To underline the message, they looked to pacts in two frontline areas in the integrating global economy -- information technology (IT) products and basic telecommunications.
And they set their sights towards a new series of talks by the year 2000 to open wider markets for farm produce and a year later on speeding up liberalisation in textiles and clothing.
Before the ministers gathered in Singapore last Monday, it was far from clear how their deliberations would turn out.
The gathering had been preceded by weeks of largely North-South wrangling at WTO headquarters in Geneva on exactly what would be on the agenda.
But although many developing countries felt left outside the core deliberations, they appeared to agree that a step forward had been achieved, if not the leap for which they had hoped.
"I think that we can say this conference has been a resounding success for all of us," said Singapore Trade Minister Yeo Cheow Tong, who chaired the gathering.
"This week has marked a real step forward for the multilateral trading system," said a delighted WTO Director-General Renato Ruggiero.
Ruggiero, 66, whose own role as an international mediator and facilitator was clearly strengthened, spoke at a final news conference of how its outcome could affect the poorest "man in the street".
If the telecoms deal is now reached as seems likely by the February 15 deadline, he said, this could mean "a telephone in every village -- for many, a matter of life and death".
The conference, formally the highest authority for the WTO, was the first real test of how the two-year-old body would hang together in the pressure-cooker atmosphere of top-level haggling.
But many delegates, including jaded envoys from its Geneva headquarters, agreed it had stood the test.

"There was a lot of anger, and many of us felt that Ruggiero was himself pushing us harder on things we didn't want than he should as a formally neutral official," said one developing country ambassador.
"But in the end, I think we have accepted that if the momentum towards ever wider liberalisation is to be kept up, it has to be driven hard."
The WTO chief himself said he was sure all members now accepted that the way ahead for both rich and poor states was through "further liberalisation".
Just how this will be managed is not exactly clear.
There were calls in Singapore for a new "trade round" -- the "Millenium Round" as proposed by European Union Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan -- at the start of the new century.

Acting United States Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky, perhaps recalling the painful struggle in the Uruguay Round from 1986 to 1993 to balance interests across a wide range of issues, clearly thought this was a bad idea.
The IT deal, negotiated almost entirely separately from other unrelated issues, showed that major trade liberalisation accords could be achieved without a round, she argued.
Ruggiero, ever the Neapolitan optimist, saw little difference. "Round or no round," he declared at his final Singapore news conference, "we will go ahead down the free trade road."
